documentNotes.title: INSTRUCTIONS
documentNotes.statement:
DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example, Doe, Jamie / Q1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Each of the four questions is worth 25 points. The questions are not necessarily of the same difficulty.

**Possibly Useful Information**

Gravitational field at the Earth’s surface $g=9.8\ N/kg$

Newton’s gravitational constant $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ N\cdot m^2/kg^2$

Binomial expansion $(1+x)^n\approx1+nx$ for $|x|\ll1$

Moment of Inertia about Center of Mass – Uniform Object (will not be provided on the second screening exam)

| Object | Moment of Inertia |
| --- | --- |
| Disk | $\frac12MR^2$ |
| Sphere | $\frac25MR^2$ |
| Rod | $\frac1{12}ML^2$ |

problems.statement:
A 4.00-meter long catapult, hinged at ground level, is used to fire large rocks as shown in the diagram at the right. A rock starts from rest with the catapult arm horizontal and is accelerated uniformly until it is released when the catapult arm makes an angle of $(\pi/3)\ rad$ ($=60^\circ$) with respect to the horizontal and the rock has a tangential velocity of 10.0 m/s.

![Catapult of length4.00m at pi/3, initial ground position X.](#p1-fig1-astra-r6-20260925)

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: How far from the original starting position (marked with an X in the diagram) does the rock land? The ground is level. Assume air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What was the angular acceleration of the rock before its release?

solution.statement:
**a.** The tangential velocity of the rock as it leaves the catapult is the initial velocity of the projectile $v_0=v_T=10.0\ m/s$ with $\theta_0=(\pi/6)$ **[1+1]**

First find the x- and y-components of the rock’s position and velocity as it leaves the catapult arm and becomes a projectile. See the accompanying figure. Taking the point marked X as the origin

![Catapult launch geometry, velocity components, angles and coordinates.](#p1-sol-fig1-astra-r6-20260925)

$x_0=R(1-\cos(\pi/3))=(4.00\ m)(1-0.5)=2.00\ m$ **[1]**

$y_0=R\sin(\pi/3)=(4.00\ m)(0.866)=3.46\ m$ **[1]**

$v_{0x}=v_0\cos(\pi/6)=(10.0\ m/s)(0.866)=8.66\ m/s$ **[1]**

$v_{0y}=v_0\sin(\pi/6)=(10.0\ m/s)(0.500)=5.00\ m/s$ **[1]**

The equations for the x and y position of the rock are:

$x=x_0+v_{0x}t$ **[2]**

$y=y_0+v_{0y}t+(\frac12)a_yt^2$ **[2]**

with $a_y=-9.8\ m/s^2$ and $y=0$ for the vertical position of the rocks landing point. **[1+1]**

Substituting $y=0$ into the y-equation,

$0=(\frac12)a_yt^2+v_{0y}t+y_0$ **[1]**

solving the quadratic equation for t and retaining only the positive t solution

$$t=\frac{-v_{0y}\pm\sqrt{v_{0y}^2-4(\frac12)a_yy_0}}{2(\frac12)a_y}=\frac{-5.00\ m/s\pm\sqrt{(5.00\ m/s)^2-2(-9.8\ m/s^2)(3.46\ m)}}{-9.8\ m/s^2}=1.49\ s$$

**[2]**

$x=x_0+v_{0x}t=2.00\ m+(8.66\ m/s)(1.49\ s)=15\ m$ **[2]**

**b.** The angular velocity of the rock at the point of release is:

$\omega=\frac{v_T}{R}=\frac{10.0\ m/s}{4.00\ m}=2.50\ rad/s$ **[2]**

Using $\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha\theta$ **[2]**

with: $\omega_0=0$, $\theta=(\pi/3)\ rad$ **[1+1]**

$$\alpha=\frac{\omega^2-\omega_0^2}{2\theta}=\frac{(2.5\ rad/s)^2-0}{2(\pi/3)}=2.98\ rad/s^2$$

**[2]**

problems.statement:
An accelerometer consists of a ball of mass $m$ attached to one end of a string. The other end of the string is attached to a cart of mass $M$. When the cart rolls down an inclined plane of angle $\theta$ with respect to the horizontal, the string makes a constant angle of $2\theta/3$ with respect to the vertical. See diagram at the right. Express your answers to the following in terms of known and given quantities. Assume air resistance is negligible.

![Cart M on slope theta carrying hanging ball m; string angle2theta/3.](#p2-fig1-astra-r6-20260925)

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the acceleration of the cart?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the coefficient of friction between the cart and the plane?

solution.statement:
**a.** Resolving the string tension $T$ and the ball weight $mg$ into components parallel and perpendicular to the plane as shown in the diagram at the right.

![Forces on the accelerometer ball resolved parallel and perpendicular to the slope.](#p2-sol-fig1-astra-r6-20260925-v2)

[1 point for each correct force/component] **[6]**

we have for the perpendicular component: $\sum F_\perp=0$ **[1]**

$T\cos(\theta/3)=mg\cos\theta$ (2.1) **[1]**

And for the parallel component: $\sum F_\parallel=ma$ **[1]**

$mg\sin\theta-T\sin(\theta/3)=ma$ (2.2) **[1]**

Solving (2.1) for $T$ $T=mg\frac{\cos\theta}{\cos(\theta/3)}$ **[1]**

and substituting into (2.2):

$mg\sin\theta-mg\frac{\cos\theta\sin(\theta/3)}{\cos(\theta/3)}=ma$ **[1]**

$a=g\left(\sin\theta-\cos\theta\frac{\sin(\theta/3)}{\cos(\theta/3)}\right)$ (2.3) **[1]**

(While it is not required to simplify the above to obtain full credit, it equals $a=2g\sin(\theta/3)$.)

**b.** The diagram to the right shows the forces acting on the cart-accelerometer system.

![Forces on cart and accelerometer: normal, friction, weight and components.](#p2-sol-fig2-astra-r6-20260925)

[1 point for each correct force/component] **[5]**

For the perpendicular component: $\sum F_\perp=0$ **[1]**

$F_n-(m+M)g\cos\theta=0$ (2.4) **[1]**

And for the parallel component:

$\sum F_\parallel=(m+M)a$ **[1]**

$(m+M)g\sin\theta-\mu F_n=(m+M)a$ (2.5) **[1]**

Combining equations (2.3), (2.4), and (2.5)

$$(m+M)g\sin\theta-\mu(m+M)g\cos\theta=(m+M)g\left[\sin\theta-\cos\theta\frac{\sin(\theta/3)}{\cos(\theta/3)}\right]$$

**[1]**

Dividing through by $(m+M)g$

$\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta=\sin\theta-\cos\theta\frac{\sin(\theta/3)}{\cos(\theta/3)}$ **[1]**

Solving for the coefficient of friction $\mu$:

$\mu=\frac{\sin(\theta/3)}{\cos(\theta/3)}=\tan(\theta/3)$

(Or any equivalent answer.) **[1]**

problems.statement: A uniform thin rod of length $L$ and mass $M$ is free to swing in a vertical plane about a frictionless horizontal axis through its upper end. Express your answers to Parts (a) and (b) in terms of $M,L$, and $g$. Assume air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: The rod is released from rest in a horizontal position. Find its angular velocity at the moment it reaches a vertical orientation.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Suppose at this moment its bottom end collides totally inelastically with a stationary point mass $M$ (the same mass as that of the rod). The point mass sticks to the rod. What is the angular velocity just after the collision?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Numerically evaluate the maximum angle (with respect to the vertical) the rod attains after the collision.

solution.statement:
**a.** The rotational inertia of a uniform thin rod about its end is found using the parallel axis theorem:

$I=I_{cm}+M(L/2)^2=(\frac1{12})ML^2+(\frac14)ML^2=(\frac13)ML^2$ **[2]**

Using energy conservation: $K_0+U_0=K_F+U_F$ **[2]**

Let the lowest position of the rod’s center of mass ($L/2$ below the axis) be the zero of gravitational potential energy. Then $U_0=Mg(L/2)$ and $U_F=0$ **[1+1]**

For kinetic energy: $K_0=0$, $K_F=(1/2)I\omega^2$ **[1+1]**

Substitution into the energy conservation equation yields

$Mg(L/2)=(\frac12)(\frac13)ML^2\omega^2$. **[1]**

Dividing by $M,L$, and $1/2$

$g=(\frac13)L\omega^2$

or $\omega=\sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}$ **[1]**

**b.** The collision is inelastic. Using angular momentum conservation

$I_0\omega_0=I_F\omega_F$ **[2]**

Only the rod is moving initially, so $I_0=(\frac13)ML^2$ and $\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}$ **[1+1]**

The final rotational inertia is the sum of the rod’s and point mass’s

$I_F=(\frac13)ML^2+ML^2=(\frac43)ML^2$ **[2]**

Therefore:

$$\omega_F=\omega_0\frac{I_0}{I_F}=\sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}\left(\frac{(\frac13)ML^2}{(\frac43)ML^2}\right)=\left(\frac14\right)\sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}$$

**[2]**

**c.** Once the collision is over, mechanical energy is again conserved. Equating total mechanical energy immediately after the collision and at the highest point

$K_0+U_0=K_F+U_F$

![Rod and attached point mass at angle theta, with vertical rises h and h-prime.](#p3-sol-fig1-astra-r6-20260925-v2)

At the highest point $K_F=0$ **[1]**

$$K_0=(\tfrac12)I\omega^2=(\tfrac12)(\tfrac43)ML^2\left((\tfrac14)\sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}\right)^2=(\tfrac18)MgL$$

**[1]**

Choosing the lowest point as the zero of gravitational potential energy, $U_0=0$.

In swinging to an angle $\theta$, the center of mass of the rod (marked by an x in the diagram) has moved up a distance $h'=(L/2)(1-\cos\theta)$, **[1]**

While the point mass at the end has moved up $h=L(1-\cos\theta)$. **[1]**

Therefore the final potential energy is

$$U_F=Mgh'+Mgh=Mg(L/2)(1-\cos\theta)+MgL(1-\cos\theta)=(3/2)MgL(1-\cos\theta).$$

**[1]**

Substituting into the energy conservation equation

$(\frac18)MgL=(\frac32)MgL(1-\cos\theta)$ **[1]**

$(\frac1{12})=1-\cos\theta$

$\theta=\cos^{-1}(\frac{11}{12})=0.41\ rad$ **[1]**

figures.alt: Rod and attached point mass at angle theta, with vertical rises h and h-prime.

problems.statement:
A pendulum consists of a small metal sphere of mass $M$ attached to a 0.60-m massless string. It hangs from a support that is located 0.30 m to the right of and 0.40 m above a fixed small rod oriented perpendicular to the plane of swing. Assume that there is no friction between the rod and the string and ignore air resistance. The pendulum is pulled to the right and released from rest when the bob is located 0.15 m higher than the rod (See Fig. 1). As the pendulum swings to the left, the string contacts the rod and the sphere begins to loop around it (See Fig. 2). Ignore the diameter of the rod and take $y$ to be the height of the sphere above the rod. Express your answers to the following in terms of $y,M$, and $g$.

![Fig.1: Initial pendulum position with support and rod offsets and bob height.](#p4-fig1-astra-r6-20260925)

![Fig.2: String contacting rod and bob of mass M at height y.](#p4-fig2-astra-r6-20260925)

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find an expression for the tension $T$ in the string when the string is in contact with the rod.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the x- and y-components of the force that the rod exerts on the string.

solution.statement:
![Pendulum contacting rod: tension forces, weight, radius0.10m and geometry.](#p4-sol-fig1-astra-r6-20260925)

**a.** Applying energy conservation between the initial point $h_0=0.15\ m$ and the point $y$

$K_0+U_0=K_y+U_y$ **[2]**

Initially $K_0=0$, $U_0=Mgh_0$ **[1+1]**

At point $y$ $K_y=(\frac12)Mv^2$, $U_y=Mgy$ **[1+1]**

$Mgh_0=(\frac12)Mv^2+Mgy$ (4.1) **[1]**

The sphere is moving in a circle of radius

$R=0.60\ m-\sqrt{(0.40\ m)^2+(0.30\ m)^2}=0.10\ m$. **[1]**

The total centripetal force has two contributions, the tension in the string $T$ and the radial component of the sphere’s weight, $Mg\cos\theta$. Setting the total centripetal force equal to the mass times the centripetal acceleration

$T+Mg\cos\theta=M\frac{v^2}{R}$ (4.2) **[4]**

Solving (4.1) for $Mv^2$ and substituting into (4.2)

$T+Mg\cos\theta=\frac{2Mg(h_0-y)}{R}$, (4.3) **[1]**

From the geometry $\cos\theta=\frac yR$. **[1]**

Combining with (4.3) and solving for $T$

$$T=\frac{2Mg(h_0-y)}R-Mg\frac yR=\frac{Mg(2h_0-3y)}R=\frac{Mg(0.30m-3y)}{0.10m}$$

$T=3Mg(1-10y)$ where y is in meters. **[1]**

**b.** By Newton’s third law, $F$, the force the rod exerts on the string, is equal and opposite to the force the string exerts on the rod. If there is no friction between the rod and the string, then the tension in both string segments is the same $T$.

$F_x=-\sum T_{sx}=-(T\sin36.9^\circ-T\sin\theta)$ **[2]**

and $F_y=-\sum T_{sy}=-(T\cos36.9^\circ+T\cos\theta)$. **[2]**

Since $\cos\theta=\frac yR$, $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-(\frac yR)^2}$ **[1+1]**

$F_x=-T\left(0.60-\sqrt{1-(\frac yR)^2}\right)$ **[1]**

$F_x=-3Mg(1-10y)\left[0.60-\sqrt{1-(10y)^2}\right]$ y in meters. **[1]**

$F_y=-T\left(0.80+\frac yR\right)$ **[1]**

$F_y=-3Mg(1-10y)(0.80+10y)$ y in meters. **[1]**
